items.headline: Autodesk Flow Studio solves AI video's biggest challenge – creative control
items.body_text:
We've reached the point where AI video can generate some genuinely stunning shots. Landscapes, characters, cinematic camera angles, whole scenes that would have taken a small team to put together not so long ago are appearing in seconds. But anyone who's tried to turn those impressive clips into something resembling an actual film has probably run into the same problem: it's much easier to get AI to create something short and simple than it is to direct something long-form and meaningful.

That's the problem Autodesk is trying to solve with the latest expansion of Autodesk Flow Studio, which it now describes as an AI-native creative platform rather than simply another generative AI tool. Instead of asking you to describe everything in a prompt and hoping the model fills in the gaps, the new 3D Editor + Canvas workflow first puts cameras, characters, animation, environments and AI motion-capture data into a proper 3D workspace, leaving AI to generate and refine the finished visuals.

Ironically, Autodesk's answer to AI isn't more AI. Instead, it's putting creators back into a production workflow they'll already recognise. "Because filmmaking has always been directed in 3D, even though most generative AI video workflows have tried to control it through 2D inputs," says Nikola Todorovic, co-founder of Wonder Dynamics, an Autodesk company. "In the real world, a director works spatially. You direct an actor where to move, where to look, how quickly to perform an action, and how they relate to the camera and the environment. You place the camera, shape its movement, adjust the framing, and refine the timing. These are all decisions made in three-dimensional space."

With 3D Editor, creators can block scenes, direct performances, and control timing, pacing, and camera movement before moving into Canvas to generate, refine, and shape the final look in 2D. "With 3D Editor, creators can make those filmmaking decisions explicitly and refine them with precision before generating the final image," Todorovic says.

Canvas itself serves as a familiar node-based editor, allowing creators to experiment with AI image and video models after the scene has been assembled, effectively separating direction from rendering. Autodesk says creators can stay entirely in the faster 2D workflow if that's all they need, or move into 3D when they want more precise control over composition, cameras and scene construction.

"The goal is to give creators flexibility," says Todorovic. "They can stay in 2D when they want speed and simplicity or move into 3D when a shot requires more precise direction."

After watching the demo (below), it's hard to argue with where Autodesk is taking its AI platform. Rather than another parade of prompts magically becoming videos, Todorovic started with footage of someone walking. Flow Studio extracted the performance, converted it into animation and applied it to a robot created in Wonder 3D, while also lifting the camera movement from the original clip. The result means you're no longer looking at a single AI-generated sequence; you're looking at a performance, a camera move and a character that can all be reused independently. As Todorovic joked during the demo, the result was "this little sad bot just wandering into the void, questioning his existence."

From there, the robot was dropped into a city generated by World Labs Marble. Then the city became a sci-fi landscape. Then an alleyway. The animation never changed. Neither did the camera. Only the world around the character did, and that's where this starts feeling like an actual production workflow. You're no longer throwing prompts at a model and hoping for the best; you're making creative decisions about individual parts of a scene, much as you would in Maya or Blender.

The demo even flipped the process around, starting with an environment rather than a character. Todorovic wandered through a generated garage, found a camera angle he liked, built the shot first and only then dropped a character into the scene. It's a small detail, but it says a lot about where Autodesk thinks AI filmmaking is heading, with prompts becoming less important than scene direction.

That shift also reflects Autodesk's view that traditional production skills won't disappear in an AI workflow. "I don't think 3D skills become mandatory, but I do think they become more valuable," says Todorovic. "The goal is to give creators flexibility. They can stay in 2D when they want speed and simplicity or move into 3D when they need more precise direction. For people who already understand 3D space, skills such as camera blocking, staging, composition, and animation can now have an even greater creative payoff."

For the last couple of years, AI companies have been competing on who can generate the prettiest image or the most convincing five-second clip, but those demos often fall apart the moment you want to direct something specific. As Todorovic puts it, "We get quickly to 80% completion of the shot, but getting control in the last 20%, especially around iteration, is where these 2D-only approaches break."

Autodesk is instead betting that the next stage isn't better generation; it's better control, and that's a far more interesting idea because it puts composition, cinematography, staging and animation back at the centre of the creative process rather than asking AI to make every decision. I've spoken to a number of filmmakers in the last year who have been experimenting with AI, including Kavan Cardoza and Kévin Mendiboure, and they say the same thing: AI is a tool, but you still need knowledge of film techniques and editing to make anything meaningful.

Autodesk says the new workflow is aimed at everyone from independent filmmakers and artists to studios, marketers and storytellers looking to build more complex productions. That accessibility is intentional. "One of the biggest opportunities is for independent filmmakers and small creative teams to take on work that previously required a much larger production infrastructure," says Todorovic. "A single artist or small team can now explore, iterate, and execute at a scale that would previously have been difficult to reach."

Autodesk also says that deeper Maya integration, broader asset import, AI-assisted scene construction, and agent-driven directing workflows are all on the roadmap.

The bigger lesson is already here, though. Autodesk's argument isn't that prompts disappear, but that they stop being the centre of the creative process. Instead, 3D becomes the place where filmmakers make decisions, where foundational knowledge informs those decisions, and where AI becomes the technology that renders them. "We're moving from AI as an asset and video generator toward AI as a genuine creative assistant," says Todorovic. "The most useful AI will not replace creative decision-making; it will make those decisions faster to explore and easier to realise."

If that's where generative filmmaking is heading, it's a much more interesting future than simply 'getting good' at typing prompts.

Visit Flow Studio for more information.

items.headline: Backflip AI updated engine flips mesh into feature tree-CAD model in seconds
items.body_text:
Backflip AI's copilot has had an extensive reworking to its foundational model for AI, allowing it to reverse engineer a part into fully editable parametric CAD, with a feature tree as though built and by your best human engineers.

Capable of converting 3D scans data, STLs, and other mesh files into fully editable, parametric CAD models, Backflip AI says that the update on its exiting Mesh-to-CAD AI excels at moderate-complexity 3-axis CNC milled and turned parts.

The data can then be pushed straight into a user's CAD package, where it's fully editable. Agent loops layered on top of the model take this further – the 3D Scan to CAD tool can reconstruct a mesh, check its own work, then iterate to improve fidelity and dimensional accuracy.

Two modes are available; a Fast mode that reconstructs typical geometries in a couple of minutes; and Thinking mode that gives the agent more time to work through complex geometry for higher-fidelity results.

The software also includes a Multimodal AI Search capable of trawling a parts library from text prompts or photo images to instantly find a part you need.

Available today as an Autodesk Fusion add-in and on the web, plugins for additional CAD packages are in development and coming later this year. Continued access starts at $20 per month across Builder, Pro, Business, and Enterprise plans.

"Most frontier models have limited 3D comprehension that emerges more or less as a byproduct of their training on large-scale internet data. We built ours with 3D CAD operations as a first-class primitive and trained it to design the way engineers actually do – breaking down a bulk geometry, then rebuilding it feature by feature, operation by operation," said Backflip founding engineer Kairo Morton.

"The result is the first foundation model whose output you can open in your CAD package and just keep working. Today, that unlocks scan to CAD, and it's the base on which everything we build next stands."

Until now, turning any physical part into a usable CAD model has meant hours of skilled reverse-engineering work at a typical cost of $1,500 or more per part, says Backflip AI, stating that its latest tools can reduce that figure to roughly $10 – a more than 100x drop that makes it economical for manufacturers to digitise every part on the factory floor rather than a fraction of them.

"Star Trek had the replicator: a machine that creates anything. We built the reverse. It takes anything real and creates a digital version you can make, modify, or improve," said Backflip AI CEO Greg Mark. "When something breaks, [factory staff] have to start by reverse engineering it — making it digital. It's an hours-to-days-long process that costs about $1,500 per part. Our new AI model does it for about $10, in one to five minutes," adding that this will free up more talented CAD engineers to design more important parts, speed up factory floor efficiencies and enable more skilled people to use CAD.

items.headline: Give your eve agent a browser
items.body_text:
Your eve agent can now navigate the web like a human with agent-browser.

The @agent-browser/eve extension gives any eve agent a full set of browser tools: navigate pages, read content, click, fill forms, take screenshots, and inspect console and network activity. Everything runs inside the agent's sandbox.

Install the extension:

pnpm add @agent-browser/eve

Then mount it under agent/extensions/:

agent/extensions/browser.ts

import browser from "@agent-browser/eve";

export default browser({
  allowedDomains: ["example.com", "*.example.com"],
  maxOutputChars: 50000,
});

Your agent gets namespaced tools like browser__navigate, browser__snapshot, browser__click, browser__fill, and browser__screenshot. Snapshot refs such as [ref=e12] become @e12 selectors, so the agent can inspect a page, then act on exactly what it saw.

The extension includes:

Sandbox isolation: Chromium and agent-browser run in the eve sandbox, not your app. Pre-install them in your sandbox template so sessions start warm, or let the extension install them on first use.

Domain allowlist: Restrict navigation and subresources with allowedDomains, and control output size, screenshot handling, proxy use, and session naming through extension options.

Credential protection: Cookie, storage, and saved-auth-state commands are never exposed to the model. Use eve extension overrides to disable tools, require approvals, or add app-specific guarded tools.

See a complete Next.js eve app with the extension mounted in the example, or read the documentation to get started.

items.headline: What your AI co-designer can't infer from your hex values
items.body_text:
It took me embarrassingly long to understand the one thing about working with design agents that now shapes how I set up almost every project. And the moment I realised what I was missing, it was almost annoying how simple it was.

When you use AI to generate a design (or create flows, or mental modals, etc) an agent hands you something that is both good and generic at the same time. Clean design, usable and user-friendly, clearly made by something that knows what it’s doing. But then you realise — it’s missing the empty state, leaning on colour alone to carry meaning, reaching for a pattern you’d specifically decided against three weeks ago and using specs don’t belong to your project. The truth is, that none of this is the agent being careless — it did a completely fair job of the brief it actually had. However, the brief was so much thinner than the one in my head.

As a fractional designer, working half-time and managing several clients at the same time, I rely on AI on multiple occasions:

Initial prep — identifying flows, brainstorming mental modals, competitive analysis, strategy brainstorm, etc.

Design system management

Files cleanup and audit

Making first drafts to solve the “blank canvas” issue and have a solid starting point to continue from.

Copy and content

As a solo designer, AI really replaces a co-designer and provides a second brain and a second pair of eyes. So with time I has come up with a system, that actually plays a role of my assistant.

Intent before everything

The design intent is the first thing to go. The agent can write React all day, but it can’t know which of your colours carries meaning and which is just decoration. It can’t know that your users misread status when it’s shown by colour alone, or that you looked hard at a modal for this exact spot last month and talked yourself out of it, for reasons you’d still stand behind today.

So the best way for AI to fill these gaps is to guess. Usually well enough to look right — which is exactly what makes the wrong bits so easy to miss. A generic answer with a confident finish reads, at a glance, like a considered one. You have to actually look to catch the difference, and by the time you’re looking, you’re already half-persuaded.

I’ve written before about this being a briefing problem more than a prompting one — that the quality ceiling isn’t set by how cleverly you phrase the ask, but by how much of your judgment is sitting in the context when you make it. The field has a name for this now — context engineering, the deliberate shift away from prompt engineering — and Anthropic’s own guidance for building agents lands in the same place: output quality is capped less by the wording of a request than by the completeness of the context around it. I’ve found it far more useful.

It’s natural to picture markdown files as documentation — the sort of thing you’d write for someone joining the team next quarter. It’s exactly why my early ones were useless. A human reader wants the story and the reasoning. They want to understand why a rule exists before they’ll trust it. An agent doesn’t want any of that. It wants a rule it can hold its own output against, right now, before it generates a single thing.

The set I’ve landed on

Press enter or click to view image in full size

How .md files are user when working with the terminal and Figma (or anothother tool) MCP

First, how I actually work, because it shapes all of this. I spend most of my time in the terminal, using a coding agent to ideate and build the designs themselves — not typing into a chat window and pasting results somewhere, but working inside the project. So these files live right where the work happens, in the folder the agent already reads. And my design system is usually wired straight into them: the design and components files carry a link to the live system, so the terminal can reach the real tokens, the real components, the real variables — not my description of them. That link is what gives the files teeth. The agent isn’t guessing at my spacing scale; it’s reading it.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Nine markdown files structure

Over enough projects the files sorted themselves into three groups, by how often the agent needs them. Here they are — walked through the way I think about them, not as a checklist to go build this afternoon. (Please don’t. I’ll come back to why.)

The always-on three load every single session, so they’re the expensive ones — every line costs attention forever, and a bloated file waters down the constraints that matter. I keep them lean on purpose.

CLAUDE.md — the root file the agent reads automatically at the start of every session. Stack, commands and folder conventions on the surface, but its real job is to point at the others: to say which files exist and when to open them. Skip this and the other eight might as well not be there, because nothing ever sends the agent to go read them.

DESIGN.md — the highest-leverage file for a designer, and the one most people write wrong by treating it as an inventory. The agent already has my hex values from the linked system. What it can't infer is where a value is allowed to go. So this is mostly boundaries and reasons: not "space-4: 16px," but "space-4 between related things, space-8 between sections, and when unsure go larger — density reads as stress for these users."

VOICE.md — the cheapest win and the most skipped. Terminology, button and label phrasing, error and empty-state wording, the words we never use. Small, but it's the difference between an empty state that sounds like me and one that greets a user with "Oops! Something went wrong."

The per-feature three get written when a piece of work kicks off and archived the moment it ships — because a stale one is worse than no file at all. The agent can’t tell it’s out of date; it reads last month’s scope as this week’s plan.

PRD.md — problem, scope, acceptance criteria, and the section that earns its place: out of scope, the explicit "not this, not now" list. Agents expand scope constantly and helpfully, and this is the only brake I've found that reliably holds.

FLOWS.md — every state the feature can be in: default, loading, empty, saving, error, blocked, and what moves you between them. Agents build the happy path because it's usually the only path anyone described. The empty state nobody remembers to design doesn't go missing if it's written here.

RESEARCH.md — findings as synthesis, never raw notes, each one linked to the rule it produced. That link is what stops an agent from cheerfully simplifying away a constraint that looks arbitrary from the outside but was hard-won on the inside.

The reference three are read on demand rather than every session, so length stops mattering.

COMPONENTS.md — the canonical answer to "does this already exist?" Left alone, an agent will build a brand-new component instead of finding the one you have — the single most common source of design-system drift I run into. What makes it work is honesty: a file that owns up to where Figma and code have drifted apart is one the agent can lean on; a neat file that's wrong just teaches it to be confidently wrong too.

DECISIONS.md — append-only, and I'm religious about that. It's the same instinct behind architecture decision records in engineering: you don't rewrite the log, you add to it. Edit the history and you delete the evidence that you already weighed an alternative and set it aside — and then that same suggestion comes wandering back a month later in a slightly different outfit.

REVIEW.md — the checklist the agent runs before it's allowed to tell me it's done, every item a yes-or-no question. This is the one that grows: same class of bug turns up twice, I add a line.

Because the system is linked and the rules are written down, the drafts come back consistent. The agent assembles my real components, wires all the specs and foundations, including spacings (which is a game changer). . So the first draft already lands on my grid, inside my system, in my voice — which means I’m polishing something that’s genuinely mine, not dragging a stranger’s guess back toward the house style. The distance between “an agent made this” and “I made this” mostly closes upstream, in the files, before a single screen gets generated.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Nine markdown files — infographic

I don’t sit down and write all nine

Producing nine hypothetical documents in one sitting might not be a great idea, since not all of them will actually survive contact with real work and you will learn almost nothing making them.

I start with two: the root file and the design file. This foundation is perfect. I let the rest arrive I see that their absence starts actually costing me something, or when I am done brainstorming.

I write them at maybe sixty percent — then let the agent finish the job of showing me what’s missing. This is the part I’ve come to genuinely enjoy. Ask it for three variations of your most complex screen, and then ignore whether they look good. Watch where they drift. Everywhere all three wander off in the same direction is a constraint your file hasn’t said out loud yet. Add the sentence, run it again. Most files settle after two or three rounds of this. The mistakes turn out to be the diagnostic — they show me, pretty precisely, the line I forgot to write, which beats finding out from a user.

The part I actually like

If the work an agent hands back feels generic, or a little off in a way I can’t name, the fix is almost never a cleverer prompt, and it’s really never a newer tool. It’s one step upstream: tell it what world it’s standing in, and give it the few rules it could never infer from your hex values. Most of what we call unreliability is a missing constraint wearing a disguise.

The best part is that none of this is a new skill you have to go learn. The states, the decisions, the things you ruled out and why are already in your your regular design workflow. Writing them for the agent is the same work, as writing them for another designer for a proper handover.

For me it made the work feel more like designing again, not less — because the deciding moved back onto a page where I could see it and change my mind, instead of happening by accident inside a re-roll I’d never be able to reconstruct. The judgment stopped leaking out of the room when I left it. It stayed on the page, waiting for me to come back.

Resources

On context, and how agents actually read it

Effective context engineering for AI agents — Anthropic. The clearest write-up of the “give the tool a world first” idea. Written for people building agents, but the principle is pure design: curate what goes in, and what comes out follows.

Context engineering — Simon Willison. The piece that named the shift for everyone outside the labs: the ceiling on output isn’t how you word the prompt, it’s the context you assemble around it.

Claude Code best practices — Anthropic. Where the CLAUDE.md convention comes from, and why the always-on file is the one worth keeping lean.

On DESIGN.md

Writing a DESIGN.md file Claude can actually use — My own deep-dive on the difference between a file AI can read and one it can reason with.

DESIGN.md Explained — Department of Product. The format reshaping how AI builds UI.

Atlassian’s DESIGN.md is here: what we learned testing portable design context — Atlassian. A big design system team testing the format for real, including where it falls short. Refreshingly honest about the limits.

designmd.ai — The emerging spec itself, if you want to see where the format is heading.

On the design fundamentals underneath

Empty states in application design — Nielsen Norman Group. Why the state nobody remembers to design is often the first one a user hits — and what a good one does. The thing FLOWS.md exists to stop an agent from skipping.

On specs, and writing decisions down

Spec-driven development with AI: Spec Kit — The GitHub Blog. The engineering cousin of these files: specify, then plan, then build. The flow makes the why click even if you never use the toolkit.

Architecture decision records — The engineering practice DECISIONS.md borrows from wholesale: record what you chose and what you rejected, append-only, so a settled debate doesn't quietly reopen a month later.

items.headline: Figma Motion basics: Keyframes
items.body_text:
Keyframes are one of two ways to animate objects in Figma Motion. A keyframe marks a point in time where you set a specific value for a layer property. When you set a second keyframe for the same property but with a different value, Figma Motion animates the transition between them.

Chapters: 00:00 Keyframe basics / 00:19 Where to set keyframes / 00:35 How to add a keyframe / 01:12 Update keyframe's value / 01:41 Loop keyframes / 01:58 Auto-keyframe

Let's learn about keyframes. Keyframes are one of two ways to animate objects in Figma motion. A keyframe marks a point in time where you set a specific value for a layer property. When you set a second keyframe for the same property but with a different value, Figma motion animates the transition between them. You can set [music] keyframes for any property with a diamond icon next to it. This includes standard properties like position, [music] scale, and rotation, as well as less obvious ones like fills, effects, and shaders. To add a keyframe, [music] click the diamond icon next to the layer property. The diamond will turn blue and a new keyframe will be added to the timeline. The layer section of the timeline indicates the type of keyframe applied [music] and the property value associated with it. To create movement, you'll need at least two keyframes for the same property. For example, if I wanted [music] this square to scale from 0 to 100% over 1,000 milliseconds, I'd add one scale keyframe to the start of the timeline with a value of 0 and a second keyframe at the 1,000 millisecond mark with a value of 100. To change a keyframe's value, double-click on it to select [music] it. Then update the value either in the right sidebar or in the layer section of the timeline. You can also copy and paste keyframes or select two keyframes on different layer tracks and right-click to align them vertically on the timeline. To delete a keyframe, select it and press delete on your keyboard. You can also loop keyframes if you'd like the motion to play continuously for the full duration of your animation. Right-click on the keyframe in the layer section and choose loop track. This copies the existing keyframes along the length of the timeline. For faster keyframe creation, you can enable auto keyframe in the timeline controls. While enabled, any change you make to an object will automatically add new keyframes to the timeline. Just drag the playhead where you want the change to occur and update the property, either by changing the value in the right sidebar or by making the change directly on the canvas. Every property you change while auto keyframe is active will be recorded. So, be sure to disable auto keyframe once you're done making changes to avoid creating unintended keyframes.
